newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco billboards not likely to disappear soon.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco billboards not likely to disappear soon.

text.p: Lawyers poring over the advertising restrictions in last week's historic tobacco agreement said on Monday that it could be years before the first Joe Camel billboard comes down.
A total ban on billboard advertising was among broad curbs on tobacco marketing agreed to Friday by major tobacco companies in order to settle smoking liability lawsuits.
The companies also agreed to limit print ads -- eliminating cartoon characters such as Joe Camel -- and restrict the public display of tobacco brand names.
Depending on how the tobacco marketing restrictions are put into effect, it could be "months, probably years" before a change is seen, said John Fithian of the Washington law firm Patton Boggs.

"The agreement specifies an enforcement time schedule to kick in nine months after passage (by Congress)," said Fithian, who represents a coalition of billboard companies, magazine publishers and advertiser groups. "I can't imagine Congress could pass this before the end of this year."

Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, predicted Monday that Congress would make major revisions in the agreement, which calls for payments totalling $368.5 billion by tobacco companies in exchange for immunity from future punitive liability for past acts. Wyden appeared on ABC's "Good Morning America."
Attorney General Michael Moore of Mississippi, a chief architect of the pact, said on the same programme that major tinkering by Congress could kill the deal.

Fithian, who represented plaintiffs in a recent successful challenge to Food and Drug Administration restrictions on tobacco advertising, was not directly involved in the talks between the tobacco companies and state attorneys general.
But he said his group was still discussing whether to mount a constitutional challenge on freedom-of-speech grounds to any law Congress might pass to restrict tobacco advertising.
"We view it as a big threat and the broadest commercial-speech censorship we've ever seen," he said.

In addition to a ban on billboard advertising, the tobacco companies agreed to limitations on print ads and so-called point-of-purchase displays in stores and a ban on sponsorship of entertainment events and tobacco logos on "gear" such as hats, lighters, bags and T-shirts.
The $2 billion outdoor billboard industry is expected to survive the loss of tobacco advertising, according to an industry representative.

Tobacco companies spent about $200 million in outdoor advertising in 1996, about 10 percent of the industry total, said Kippy Burns, vice president for communication at the Outdoor Advertising Association of America. In 1979 tobacco accounted for 30 percent of billboard advertising.
"Losing 10 percent of anyone's revenues is going to be felt," she said. "It would hurt, but it wouldn't sink the industry."
